entries.7b3bd92837089a156936a8e47e2a3a5f2e7617ab: <div sID="gen5551" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="15" osisID="1Sam.15" sID="1Sam.15"/> <div eID="gen5551" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5552" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen5553" type="x-p"/> In this chapter we have the final rejection of Saul from being king, for his disobedience to God's command in not utterly destroying the Amalekites. By his wars and victories he hoped to magnify and perpetuate his own name and honour, but, by his mismanagement of them, he ruined himself, and laid his honour in the dust. Here is, I. The commission God gave him to destroy the Amalekites, with a command to do it utterly, <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.1-1Sam.15.3">ver. 1-3</reference>. II. Saul's preparation for this expedition, <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.4-1Sam.15.6">ver. 4-6</reference>. III. His success, and partial execution of this commission, <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.7-1Sam.15.9">ver. 7-9</reference>. IV. His examination before Samuel, and sentence passed upon him, notwithstanding the many frivolous pleas he made to excuse himself, <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.10-1Sam.15.31">ver. 10-31</reference>. V. The slaying of Agag, <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.32-1Sam.15.33">ver. 32, 33</reference>. VI. Samuel's final farewell to Saul, <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.34-1Sam.15.35">ver. 34, 35</reference>.
entries.19b3627dee9612ec3a62abc8bd15541a546dde94: <div eID="gen5553" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen5552" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Amalekites Destroyed. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1065.)</title> <div sID="gen5554" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Samuel also said unto Saul, The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> sent me to anoint thee <hi type="italic">to be</hi> king over his people, over Israel: now therefore hearken thou unto the voice of the words of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">2</hi> Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts, I remember <hi type="italic">that</hi> which Amalek did to Israel, how he laid <hi type="italic">wait</hi> for him in the way, when he came up from Egypt. <hi type="super">3</hi> Now go and smite Amalek, and utterly destroy all that they have, and spare them not; but slay both man and woman, infant and suckling, ox and sheep, camel and ass. <hi type="super">4</hi> And Saul gathered the people together, and numbered them in Telaim, two hundred thousand footmen, and ten thousand men of Judah. <hi type="super">5</hi> And Saul came to a city of Amalek, and laid wait in the valley. <hi type="super">6</hi> And Saul said unto the Kenites, Go, depart, get you down from among the Amalekites, lest I destroy you with them: for ye shewed kindness to all the children of Israel, when they came up out of Egypt. So the Kenites departed from among the Amalekites. <hi type="super">7</hi> And Saul smote the Amalekites from Havilah <hi type="italic">until</hi> thou comest to Shur, that <hi type="italic">is</hi> over against Egypt. <hi type="super">8</hi> And he took Agag the king of the Amalekites alive, and utterly destroyed all the people with the edge of the sword. <hi type="super">9</hi> But Saul and the people spared Agag, and the best of the sheep, and of the oxen, and of the fatlings, and the lambs, and all <hi type="italic">that was</hi> good, and would not utterly destroy them: but every thing <hi type="italic">that was</hi> vile and refuse, that they destroyed utterly. <div eID="gen5554" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5555" type="x-p"/> Here, I. Samuel, in God's name, solemnly requires Saul to be obedient to the command of God, and plainly intimates that he was now about to put him upon a trial, in one particular instance, whether he would be obedient or no, <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.1">v. 1</reference>. And the making of this so expressly the trial of his obedience did very much aggravate his disobedience. 1. He reminds him of what God had done for him: "<hi type="italic">The Lord sent me to anoint thee to be a king.</hi> God gave thee thy power, and therefore he expects thou shouldst use thy power for him. He put honour upon thee, and now thou must study how to do him honour. He made thee king over Israel, and now thou must plead Israel's cause and avenge their quarrels. Thou art advanced to command Israel, but know that thou art a subject to the God of Israel and must be commanded by him." Men's preferment, instead of releasing them from their obedience to God, obliges them so much the more to it. Samuel had himself been employed to anoint Saul, and therefore was the fitter to be sent with these orders to him. 2. He tells him, in general, that, in consideration of this, whatever God commanded him to do he was bound to do it: <hi type="italic">Now therefore hearken to the voice of the Lord.</hi> Note, God's favours to us lay strong obligations upon us to be obedient to him. This we must render, <reference osisRef="Ps.116.12">Ps. cxvi. 12</reference>. <div eID="gen5555" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5556" type="x-p"/> II. He appoints him a particular piece of service, in which he must now show his obedience to God more than in any thing he had done yet. Samuel premises God's authority to the command: <hi type="italic">Thus says the Lord of hosts,</hi> the Lord of all hosts, of Israel's hosts. He also gives him a reason for the command, that the severity he must use might not seem hard: <hi type="italic">I remember that which Amalek did to Israel,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.2">v. 2</reference>. God had an ancient quarrel with the Amalekites, for the injuries they did to his people Israel when he brought them out of Egypt. We have the story, <reference osisRef="Exod.17.8-Exod.17.16">Exod. xvii. 8</reference>, &c., and the crime is aggravated, <reference osisRef="Deut.25.18">Deut. xxv. 18</reference>. He basely smote the hindmost of them, and feared not God. God then swore that he would have <hi type="italic">war with Amalek from generation to generation,</hi> and that in process of time he <hi type="italic">would utterly put out the remembrance of Amalek;</hi> this is the work that Saul is now appointed to do (<reference osisRef="1Sam.15.3">v. 3</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Go and smite Amalek.</hi> Israel is now strong, and the measure of the iniquity of Amalek is now full; now go and make a full riddance of that devoted nation." He is expressly commanded to kill and slay all before him, <hi type="italic">man and woman, infant and suckling,</hi> and not spare them out of pity; also <hi type="italic">ox and sheep, camel and ass,</hi> and not spare them out of covetousness. Note, 1. Injuries done to God's Israel will certainly be reckoned for sooner or later, especially the opposition given them when they are coming out of Egypt. 2. God often bears long with those that are marked for ruin. The sentence passed is not executed speedily. 3. Though he bear long, he will not bear always. The year of recompence for the controversy of Israel will come at last. Though divine justice strikes slowly it strikes surely. 4. The longer judgment is delayed many times the more severe it is when it comes. 5. God chooses out instruments to do his work that are fittest for it. This was bloody work, and therefore Saul who was a rough and severe man must do it. <div eID="gen5556" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5557" type="x-p"/> III. Saul hereupon musters his forces, and makes a descent upon the country of Amalek. It was an immense army that he brought into the field (<reference osisRef="1Sam.15.4">v. 4</reference>): 200,000 <hi type="italic">footmen.</hi> When he came to engage the Philistines, and the success was hazardous, he had but 600 attending him, <reference osisRef="1Sam.13.15">ch. xiii. 15</reference>. But now that he was to attack the Amalekites by express order from heaven, in which he was sure of victory, he had thousands at his call. But, whatever it was at other times, it was not now for the honour of Judah that their forces were numbered by themselves, for their quota was scandalously short (whatever was the reason), but a twentieth part of the whole, for they were by 10,000, when the other ten tribes (for I except Levi) brought into the field 200 000. The day of Judah's honour drew near, but had not yet come. Saul numbered them in <hi type="italic">Telaim,</hi> which signifies <hi type="italic">lambs.</hi> He numbered then <hi type="italic">like lambs</hi> (so the vulgar Latin), numbered them <hi type="italic">by the paschal lambs</hi> (so the Chaldee), allowing ten to a lamb, a way of numbering used by the Jews in the later times of their nation. Saul drew all his forces to the <hi type="italic">city of Amalek,</hi> that city that was their metropolis (<reference osisRef="1Sam.15.5">v. 5</reference>), that he might provoke them to give him battle. <div eID="gen5557" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5558" type="x-p"/> IV. He gave friendly advice to the Kenites to separate themselves from the Amalekites among whom they dwelt, while this execution was in doing, <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.6">v. 6</reference>. Herein he did prudently and piously, and, it is probable, according to the direction Samuel gave him. The Kenites were of the family and kindred of Jethro, Moses's father-in-law, a people that dwelt in tents, which made it easy for them, upon every occasion, to remove to other lands not appropriated. Many of them, at this time, dwelt among the Amalekites, where, though they dwelt in tents, they were fortified by nature, for <hi type="italic">they put their nest in a rock,</hi> being hardy people that could live any where, and affected fastnesses, <reference osisRef="Num.24.21">Num. xxiv. 21</reference>. Balaam had foretold that they should be wasted, <reference osisRef="Num.24.22">Num. xxiv. 22</reference>. However, Saul must not waste them. But, 1. He acknowledges the kindness of their ancestors to Israel, when they came out of Egypt. Jethro and his family had been very helpful and serviceable to them in their passage through the wilderness, had been to them instead of eyes, and this is remembered to their posterity many ages after. Thus a good man leaves the divine blessing for an inheritance to his children's children; those that come after us may be reaping the benefit of our good works when we are in our graves. God is not unrighteous to forget the kindnesses shown to his people; but they shall be remembered another day, at furthest in the great day, <hi type="italic">and recompensed in the resurrection of the just. I was hungry, and you gave me meat.</hi> God's remembering the kindness of the Kenites' ancestors in favour to them, at the same time when he was punishing the injuries done by the ancestors of the Amalekites, helped to clear the righteousness of God in that dispensation. If he entail favours, why may he not entail frowns? He espouses his people's cause, so as to <hi type="italic">bless those that bless them;</hi> and therefore so as to <hi type="italic">curse those that curse them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Num.24.9">Num. xxiv. 9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.12.3">Gen. xii. 3</reference>. They cannot themselves requite the kindnesses nor avenge the injuries done them, but God will do both. 2. He desires them to remove their tents from among the Amalekites: <hi type="italic">Go, depart, get you down from among them.</hi> When destroying judgments are abroad God will take care to separate between the precious and the vile, and to hide the meek of the earth in the day of his anger. It is dangerous being found in the company of God's enemies, and it is our duty and interest to <hi type="italic">come out from among them,</hi> lest we share in their sins and plagues, <reference osisRef="Rev.18.4">Rev. xviii. 4</reference>. The Jews have a saying, <hi type="italic">Woe to the wicked man and woe to his neighbour.</hi> <div eID="gen5558" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5559" type="x-p"/> V. Saul prevailed against the Amalekites, for it was rather an execution of condemned malefactors than a war with contending enemies. The issue could not be dubious when the cause was just and the call so clear: <hi type="italic">He smote them</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Sam.15.7">v. 7</reference>), <hi type="italic">utterly destroyed them,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.8">v. 8</reference>. Now they paid dearly for the sin of their ancestors. God sometimes <hi type="italic">lays up iniquity for the children.</hi> They were idolaters, and were guilty of many other sins, for which they deserved to fall under the wrath of God; yet, when God would reckon with them, he fastened upon the sin of their ancestors in abusing his Israel as the ground of his quarrel. Lord, How unsearchable are thy judgments, yet how incontestable is thy righteousness! <div eID="gen5559" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5560" type="x-p"/> VI. Yet he did his work by halves, <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.9">v. 9</reference>. 1. He <hi type="italic">spared Agag,</hi> because he was a king like himself, and perhaps in hope to get a great ransom for him. 2. He spared the best of the cattle, and destroyed only the refuse, that was good for little. Many of the people, we may suppose, made their escape, and took their effects with them into other countries, and therefore we read of Amalekites after this; but that could not be helped. It was Saul's fault that he did not destroy such as came to his hands and were in his power. That which was now destroyed was in effect sacrificed to the justice of God, as the God to whom vengeance belongeth; and for Saul to think the torn and the sick, the lame and the lean, good enough for that, while he reserved for his own fields and his own table the firstlings and the fat, was really to honour himself more than God.
entries.0c5bf41f520a18bac148f039d011c2612c96f04c: <div eID="gen5560" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Samuel Reproves Saul; Saul Rejected of God. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1065.)</title> <div sID="gen5561" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> Then came the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> unto Samuel, saying, <hi type="super">11</hi> It repenteth me that I have set up Saul <hi type="italic">to be</hi> king: for he is turned back from following me, and hath not performed my commandments. And it grieved Samuel; and he cried unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> all night. <hi type="super">12</hi> And when Samuel rose early to meet Saul in the morning, it was told Samuel, saying, Saul came to Carmel, and, behold, he set him up a place, and is gone about, and passed on, and gone down to Gilgal. <hi type="super">13</hi> And Samuel came to Saul: and Saul said unto him, Blessed <hi type="italic">be</hi> thou of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : I have performed the commandment of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">14</hi> And Samuel said, What <hi type="italic">meaneth</hi> then this bleating of the sheep in mine ears, and the lowing of the oxen which I hear? <hi type="super">15</hi> And Saul said, They have brought them from the Amalekites: for the people spared the best of the sheep and of the oxen, to sacrifice unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God; and the rest we have utterly destroyed. <hi type="super">16</hi> Then Samuel said unto Saul, Stay, and I will tell thee what the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath said to me this night. And he said unto him, Say on. <hi type="super">17</hi> And Samuel said, When thou <hi type="italic">wast</hi> little in thine own sight, <hi type="italic">wast</hi> thou not <hi type="italic">made</hi> the head of the tribes of Israel, and the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> anointed thee king over Israel? <hi type="super">18</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> sent thee on a journey, and said, Go and utterly destroy the sinners the Amalekites, and fight against them until they be consumed. <hi type="super">19</hi> Wherefore then didst thou not obey the voice of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , but didst fly upon the spoil, and didst evil in the sight of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ? <hi type="super">20</hi> And Saul said unto Samuel, Yea, I have obeyed the voice of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and have gone the way which the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> sent me, and have brought Agag the king of Amalek, and have utterly destroyed the Amalekites. <hi type="super">21</hi> But the people took of the spoil, sheep and oxen, the chief of the things which should have been utterly destroyed, to sacrifice unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God in Gilgal. <hi type="super">22</hi> And Samuel said, Hath the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">as great</hi> delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying the voice of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ? Behold, to obey <hi type="italic">is</hi> better than sacrifice, <hi type="italic">and</hi> to hearken than the fat of rams. <hi type="super">23</hi> For rebellion <hi type="italic">is as</hi> the sin of witchcraft, and stubbornness <hi type="italic">is as</hi> iniquity and idolatry. Because thou hast rejected the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , he hath also rejected thee from <hi type="italic">being</hi> king. <div eID="gen5561" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5562" type="x-p"/> Saul is here called to account by Samuel concerning the execution of his commission against the Amalekites; and remarkable instances we are here furnished with of the strictness of the justice of God and the treachery and deceitfulness of the heart of man. We are here told, <div eID="gen5562" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5563" type="x-p"/> I. What passed between God and Samuel, in secret, upon this occasion, <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.10-1Sam.15.11">v. 10, 11</reference>. 1. God determines Saul's rejection, and acquaints Samuel with it: <hi type="italic">It repenteth me that I have set up Saul to be king.</hi> Repentance in God is not, as it is in us, a change of his mind, but a change of his method or dispensation. He does not alter his will, but wills an alteration. The change was in Saul: <hi type="italic">He has turned back from following me;</hi> this construction God put upon the partiality of his obedience, and the prevalency of his covetousness. And hereby he did himself make God his enemy. God repented that he had given Saul the kingdom and the honour and power that belonged to it: but he never repented that he had given any man wisdom and grace, and his fear and love; these gifts and callings of God are without repentance. 2. Samuel laments and deprecates it. <hi type="italic">It grieved Samuel</hi> that Saul had forfeited God's favour, and that God had resolved to cast him off; and he <hi type="italic">cried unto the Lord all night,</hi> spent a whole night in interceding for him, that this decree might not go forth against him. When others were in their beds sleeping, he was upon his knees praying and wrestling with God. He did not thus deprecate his own exclusion from the government; nor was he secretly pleased, as many a one would have been, that Saul, who succeeded him, was so soon laid aside, but on the contrary prayed earnestly for his establishment, so far was he from desiring that woeful day. The rejection of sinners is the grief of good people; God delights not in their death, nor should we. <div eID="gen5563" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5564" type="x-p"/> II. What passed between Samuel and Saul in public. Samuel, being sent of God to him with these heavy tidings, went, as Ezekiel, in <hi type="italic">bitterness of soul,</hi> to meet him, perhaps according to an appointment when Saul went forth on this expedition, for Saul had come to Gilgal (<reference osisRef="1Sam.15.12">v. 12</reference>), the place where he was made king (<reference osisRef="1Sam.11.15">ch. xi. 15</reference>), and were now he would have been confirmed if he had approved himself well in the trial of his obedience. But Samuel was informed that Saul had set up a triumphal arch, or some monument of his victory, at Carmel, a city in the mountains of Judah, seeking his own honour more than the honour of God, for he set up this place (or <hi type="italic">hand,</hi> as the word is) for himself (he had more need to have been repenting of his sin and making his peace with God than boasting of his victory), and also that he had marched in great state to Gilgal, for this seems to be intimated in the manner of expression: <hi type="italic">He has gone about, and passed on, and gone down,</hi> with a great deal of pomp and parade. There Samuel gave him the meeting, and, <div eID="gen5564" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5565" type="x-p"/> 1. Saul makes his boast to Samuel of his obedience, because that was the thing by which he was now to signalize himself (<reference osisRef="1Sam.15.13">v. 13</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Blessed be thou of the Lord,</hi> for thou sendest me upon a good errand, in which I have had great success, and <hi type="italic">I have performed the commandment of the Lord.</hi>" It is very likely, if his conscience had now flown in his face at this time and charged him with disobedience, he would not have been so forward to proclaim his obedience; for by this he hoped to prevent Samuel's reproving him. Thus sinners think, by justifying themselves, to escape being <hi type="italic">judged of the Lord;</hi> whereas the only way to do that is by <hi type="italic">judging ourselves.</hi> Those that boast most of their religion may be suspected of partiality and hypocrisy in it. <div eID="gen5565" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5566" type="x-p"/> 2. Samuel convicts him by a plain demonstration of his disobedience. "Hast thou performed the commandment of the Lord? <hi type="italic">What means then the bleating of the sheep?</hi>" <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.14">v. 14</reference>. Saul would needs have it thought that God Almighty was wonderfully beholden to him for the good service he had done; but Samuel shows him that God was so far from being a debtor to him that he had just cause of action against him, and produces for evidence the <hi type="italic">bleating of the sheep, and the lowing of the oxen,</hi> which perhaps Saul appointed to bring up the rear of his triumph, but Samuel appears to them as witnesses against him. He needed not go far to disprove his professions. The noise the cattle made (like the <hi type="italic">rust of silver,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jas.5.3">Jam. v. 3</reference>) would be a <hi type="italic">witness against him.</hi> Note, It is no new thing for the plausible professions and protestations of hypocrites to be contradicted and disproved by the most plain and undeniable evidence. Many boast of their obedience to the command of God; but what mean then their indulgence of the flesh, their love of the world, their passion and uncharitableness, and their neglect of holy duties, which witness against them? <div eID="gen5566" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5567" type="x-p"/> 3. Saul insists upon his own justification against this charge, <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.15">v. 15</reference>. The fact he cannot deny; the sheep and oxen were brought from the Amalekites. But, (1.) It was not his fault, for <hi type="italic">the people spared them;</hi> as if they durst have done it without the express orders of Saul, when they knew it was against the express orders of Samuel. Note, Those that are willing to justify themselves are commonly very forward to condemn others, and to lay the blame upon any rather than take it to themselves. Sin is a brat that nobody cares to have laid at his doors. It is the sorry subterfuge of an impenitent heart, that will not confess its guilt, to lay the blame on those that were tempters, or partners, or only followers in it. (2.) It was with a good intention: "It was <hi type="italic">to sacrifice to the Lord thy God.</hi> He is thy God, and thou wilt not be against any thing that is done, as this is, for his honour." This was a false plea, for both Saul and the people designed their own profit in sparing the cattle. But, if it had been true, it would still have been frivolous, for God hates robbery for burnt-offering. God appointed these cattle to be sacrificed to him in the field, and therefore will give those no thanks that bring them to be sacrificed at his altar; for he will be served in his own way, and according to the rule he himself has prescribed. Nor will a good intention justify a bad action. <div eID="gen5567" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5568" type="x-p"/> 4. Samuel overrules, or rather overlooks, his plea, and proceeds, in God's name, to give judgment against him. He premises his authority. What he was about to say was what the Lord had said to him (<reference osisRef="1Sam.15.16">v. 16</reference>), otherwise he would have been far from passing so severe a censure upon him. Those who complain that their ministers are too harsh with them should remember that, while they keep to the word of God, they are but messengers, and must say as they are bidden, and therefore be willing, as Saul himself here was, that they should <hi type="italic">say on.</hi> Samuel delivers his message faithfully. (1.) He reminds Saul of the honour of God had done him in making him king (<reference osisRef="1Sam.15.17">v. 17</reference>), <hi type="italic">when he was little in his own sight.</hi> God regarded the lowness of his state and rewarded the lowliness of his spirit. Note, Those that are advanced to honour and wealth ought often to remember their mean beginnings, that they may never think highly of themselves, but always study to do great things for the God that had advanced them. (2.) He lays before him the plainness of the orders he was to execute (<reference osisRef="1Sam.15.18">v. 18</reference>): <hi type="italic">The Lord sent thee on a journey;</hi> so easy was the service, and so certain the success, that it was rather to be called a <hi type="italic">journey</hi> than a <hi type="italic">war.</hi> The work was honourable, to destroy the sworn enemies of God and Israel; and had he denied himself, and set aside the consideration of his own profit so far as to have destroyed all that belonged to Amalek, he would have been no loser by it at last, nor have gone this <hi type="italic">warfare on his own charges.</hi> God would no doubt have made it up to him, so that he should have no need of spoil. And therefore, (3.) He shows him how inexcusable he was in aiming to make a profit of this expedition, and to enrich himself by it (<reference osisRef="1Sam.15.19">v. 19</reference>): <hi type="italic">"Wherefore then didst thou fly upon the spoil,</hi> and convert that to thy own use which was to have been destroyed for God's honour?" See what evil the love of money is the root of; but see what is the sinfulness of sin, and that in it which above any thing else makes it evil in the sight of the Lord. It is disobedience: <hi type="italic">Thou didst not obey the voice of the Lord.</hi> <div eID="gen5568" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5569" type="x-p"/> 5. Saul repeats his vindication of himself, as that which, in defiance of conviction, he resolved to abide by, <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.20-1Sam.15.21">v. 20, 21</reference>. He denies the charge (<reference osisRef="1Sam.15.20">v. 20</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Yea, I have obeyed,</hi> I have done all I should do;" for he had done all which he thought he needed to do, so much wiser was he in his own eyes than God himself. God bade him kill all, and yet he puts in among the instances of his obedience that he brought Agag alive, which he thought was as good as if he had killed him. Thus carnal deceitful hearts think to excuse themselves from God's commandments with their own equivalents. He insists upon it that he has <hi type="italic">utterly destroyed the Amalekites</hi> themselves, which was the main thing intended; but, as to the spoil, he owns it should have been <hi type="italic">utterly destroyed;</hi> so that he knew his <hi type="italic">Lord's will,</hi> and was under no mistake about the command. But he thought that would be wilful waste; the cattle of the Midianites was taken for a prey in Moses's time (<reference osisRef="Num.31.32-Num.31.34">Num. xxxi. 32</reference>, &c.), and why not the cattle of the Amalekites now? Better it should be prey to the Israelites than to the fowls of the air and the wild beasts; and therefore he connived at the people's carrying it away. But it was their doing and not his; and, besides, it was for <hi type="italic">sacrifice to the Lord</hi> here at Gilgal, whither they were now bringing them. See what a hard thing it is to convince the children of disobedience of their sin and to strip them of their fig-leaves. <div eID="gen5569" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5570" type="x-p"/> 6. Samuel gives a full answer to his apology, since he did insist upon it, <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.22-1Sam.15.23">v. 22, 23</reference>. He appeals to his own conscience: <hi type="italic">Has the Lord as great delight in sacrifices as in obedience?</hi> Though Saul was not a man of any great acquaintance with religion, yet he could not but know this, (1.) That nothing is so pleasing to God as obedience, no, not sacrifice and offering, and the fat of rams. See here what we should seek and aim at in all the exercises of religion, even acceptance with God, that he may delight in what we do. If God be well pleased with us and our services, we are happy, we have gained our point, but otherwise <hi type="italic">to what purpose is it?</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.1.11">Isa. i. 11</reference>. Now here we are plainly told that humble, sincere, and conscientious obedience to the will of God, is more pleasing and acceptable to him than all <hi type="italic">burnt-offerings and sacrifices.</hi> A careful conformity to moral precepts recommends us to God more than all ceremonial observances, <reference osisRef="Mic.6.6-Mic.6.8">Mic. vi. 6-8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.6.6">Hos. vi. 6</reference>. Obedience is enjoyed by the eternal law of nature, but sacrifice only by a positive law. Obedience was the law of innocency, but sacrifice supposes sin come into the world, and is but a feeble attempt to take that away which obedience would have prevented. God is more glorified and self more denied by obedience than by sacrifice. It is much easier to bring a bullock or lamb to be burnt upon the altar than to bring <hi type="italic">every high thought into obedience</hi> to God and the will subject to his will. Obedience is the glory of angels (<reference osisRef="Ps.103.20">Ps. ciii. 20</reference>), and it will be ours. (2.) That nothing is so provoking to God as disobedience, setting up our wills in competition with his. This is here called <hi type="italic">rebellion</hi> and <hi type="italic">stubbornness,</hi> and is said to be as bad as <hi type="italic">witchcraft</hi> and <hi type="italic">idolatry,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.23">v. 23</reference>. It is as bad to set up other gods as to live in disobedience to the true God. Those that are governed by their own corrupt inclinations, in opposition to the command of God, do, in effect, consult the <hi type="italic">teraphim</hi> (as the word here is for idolatry) or the diviners. It was disobedience that made us all sinners (<reference osisRef="Rom.5.19">Rom. v. 19</reference>), and this is the malignity of sin, that it is the <hi type="italic">transgression of the law,</hi> and consequently it is <hi type="italic">enmity to God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.8.7">Rom. viii. 7</reference>. Saul was a king, but if he disobey the command of God, his royal dignity and power will not excuse him from the guilt of rebellion and stubbornness. It is not the rebellion of the people against their prince, but of a prince against God, that this text speaks of. <div eID="gen5570" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5571" type="x-p"/> 7. He reads his doom: in short, "<hi type="italic">Because thou has rejected the word of the Lord,</hi> hast <hi type="italic">despised it</hi> (so the Chaldee), hast <hi type="italic">made nothing of it</hi> (so the LXX.), hast cast off the government of it, therefore he has <hi type="italic">rejected thee,</hi> despised and made nothing of thee, but cast thee off <hi type="italic">from being king.</hi> He that made thee king has determined to unmake thee again." Those are unfit and unworthy to rule over men who are not willing that God should rule over them.
entries.f0be0d08761f46c64b26dc32ce4ea22f160b3daa: <div eID="gen5571" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Saul's Dethronement Foretold. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1065.)</title> <div sID="gen5572" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">24</hi> And Saul said unto Samuel, I have sinned: for I have transgressed the commandment of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and thy words: because I feared the people, and obeyed their voice. <hi type="super">25</hi> Now therefore, I pray thee, pardon my sin, and turn again with me, that I may worship the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">26</hi> And Samuel said unto Saul, I will not return with thee: for thou hast rejected the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath rejected thee from being king over Israel. <hi type="super">27</hi> And as Samuel turned about to go away, he laid hold upon the skirt of his mantle, and it rent. <hi type="super">28</hi> And Samuel said unto him, The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath rent the kingdom of Israel from thee this day, and hath given it to a neighbour of thine, <hi type="italic">that is</hi> better than thou. <hi type="super">29</hi> And also the Strength of Israel will not lie nor repent: for he <hi type="italic">is</hi> not a man, that he should repent. <hi type="super">30</hi> Then he said, I have sinned: <hi type="italic">yet</hi> honour me now, I pray thee, before the elders of my people, and before Israel, and turn again with me, that I may worship the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God. <hi type="super">31</hi> So Samuel turned again after Saul; and Saul worshipped the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <div eID="gen5572" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5573" type="x-p"/> Saul is at length brought to put himself into the dress of the penitent; but it is too evident that he only acts the part of a penitent, and is not one indeed. Observe, <div eID="gen5573" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5574" type="x-p"/> I. How poorly he expressed his repentance. It was with much ado that he was made sensible of his fault, and not till he was threatened with being deposed. This touched him in a tender part. Then he began to relent, and not till then. When Samuel told him he was <hi type="italic">rejected from being king,</hi> then he said, <hi type="italic">I have sinned,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.24">v. 24</reference>. His confession was not free nor ingenuous, but extorted by the rack, and forced from him. We observe here several bad signs of the hypocrisy of his repentance, and that it came short even of Ahab's. 1. He made his application to Samuel only, and seemed most solicitous to stand right in his opinion and to gain his favour. He makes a little god of him, only to preserve his reputation with the people, because they all knew Samuel to be a prophet, and the man that had been the instrument of his preferment. Thinking it would please Samuel, and be a sort of bribe to him, he puts it into his confession: <hi type="italic">I have transgressed the commandment of the Lord and thy word;</hi> as if he had been in God's stead, <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.24">v. 24</reference>. David, though convinced by the ministry of Nathan, yet, in his confession, has his eye to God alone, not to Nathan. <reference osisRef="Ps.51.4">Ps. li. 4</reference> <hi type="italic">Against thee only have I sinned.</hi> But Saul, ignorantly enough, confesses his sin as a transgression of Samuel's word; whereas his word was no other than a declaration of the <hi type="italic">commandment of the Lord.</hi> He also applies to Samuel for forgiveness (<reference osisRef="1Sam.15.25">v. 25</reference>): <hi type="italic">I pray thee, pardon my sin;</hi> as if any could forgive sin but God only. Those wretchedly deceive themselves who, when they have fallen into scandalous sin, think it enough to make their peace with the church and their ministers, by the show and plausible profession of repentance, without taking care to make their peace with God by the sincerity of it. The most charitable construction we can put upon this of Saul is to suppose that he looked upon Samuel as a sort of mediator between him and God, and intended an address to God in his application to him. However, it was very weak. 2. He excused his fault even in the confession of it, and that is never the fashion of a true penitent (<reference osisRef="1Sam.15.24">v. 24</reference>): I did it <hi type="italic">because I feared the people, and obeyed their voice.</hi> We have reason enough to think that it was purely his own doing and not the people's; however, if they were forward to do it, it is plain, by what we have read before, that he knew how to keep up his authority among them and did not stand in any awe of them. So that the excuse was false and frivolous; whatever he pretended, he did not really fear the people. But it is common for sinners, in excusing their faults, to plead the thoughts and workings of their own minds, because those are things which, how groundless soever, no man can disprove; but they forget that God searchest the heart. 3. All his care was to save his credit, and preserve his interest in the people, lest they should revolt from him, or at least despise him. Therefore he courts Samuel with so much earnestness (<reference osisRef="1Sam.15.25">v. 25</reference>) to turn again with him, and assist in a public thanksgiving for the victory. Very importunate he was in this matter when he laid hold on the skirt of his mantle to detain him (<reference osisRef="1Sam.15.27">v. 27</reference>), not that he cared for Samuel, but he feared that if Samuel forsook him the people would do so too. Many seem zealously affected to good ministers and good people only for the sake of their own interest and reputation, while in heart they hate them. But his expression was very gross when he said (<reference osisRef="1Sam.15.30">v. 30</reference>), <hi type="italic">I have sinned, yet honour me, I pray thee, before my people.</hi> Is this the language of a penitent? No, but the contrary: "<hi type="italic">I have sinned,</hi> shame me now, for to me belongs shame, and no man can loathe me so much as I loathe myself." Yet how often do we meet with the copies of this hypocrisy of Saul! It is very common for those who are convicted of sin to show themselves very solicitous to be honoured before the people. Whereas he that has lost the honour of an innocent can pretend to no other than that of a penitent, and it is the honour of a penitent to take shame to himself. <div eID="gen5574" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5575" type="x-p"/> II. How little he got by these thin shows of repentance. What point did he gain by them? 1. Samuel repeated the sentence passed upon him, so far was he from giving any hopes of the repeal of it, <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.26">v. 26</reference>, the same with <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.23">v. 23</reference>. <hi type="italic">He that covers his sins shall never prosper,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.28.13">Prov. xxviii. 13</reference>. Samuel refused to turn back with him, but <hi type="italic">turned about to go away,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.27">v. 27</reference>. As the thing appeared to him upon the first view, he thought it altogether unfit for him so far to countenance one whom God had rejected as to join with him in giving thanks to God for a victory which was made to serve rather Saul's covetousness than God's glory. Yet afterwards he did turn again with him (<reference osisRef="1Sam.15.31">v. 31</reference>), upon further thoughts, and probably by divine direction, either to prevent a mutiny among the people or perhaps not to do honour to Saul (for, though Saul worshipped the Lord, <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.31">v. 31</reference>, it is not said Samuel presided in that worship), but to do justice on Agag, <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.32">v. 32</reference>. 2. He illustrated the sentence by a sign, which Saul himself, by his rudeness, gave occasion for. When Samuel was turning from him he tore his clothes to detain him (<reference osisRef="1Sam.15.27">v. 27</reference>), so loth was he to part with the prophet; but Samuel put a construction upon this accident which none but a prophet could do. He made it to signify the <hi type="italic">rending of the kingdom</hi> from him (<reference osisRef="1Sam.15.28">v. 28</reference>), and that, like this, was his own doing. "He hath rent it from thee, and <hi type="italic">given it to a neighbour better than thou,</hi>" namely, to David, who afterwards, upon occasion, cut off the skirt of Saul's robe (<reference osisRef="1Sam.24.4">1 Sam. xxiv. 4</reference>), upon which Saul said (<reference osisRef="1Sam.24.20">1 Sam. xxiv. 20</reference>), <hi type="italic">I know that thou shalt surely be king,</hi> perhaps remembering this sign, the tearing of the skirt of Samuel's mantle. 3. He ratified it by a solemn declaration of its being irreversible (<reference osisRef="1Sam.15.29">v. 29</reference>): <hi type="italic">The Strength of Israel will not lie.</hi> The <hi type="italic">Eternity</hi> or <hi type="italic">Victory of Israel,</hi> so some read it; <hi type="italic">the holy One,</hi> so the Arabic; <hi type="italic">the most noble One,</hi> so the Syriac; the <hi type="italic">triumphant King of Israel,</hi> so bishop Patrick. "He is determined to depose thee, and he will not change his purpose. <hi type="italic">He is not a man that should repent.</hi>" Men are fickle and alter their minds, feeble and cannot effect their purposes; something happens which they could not foresee, by which their measures are broken. But with God it is not so. God has sometimes repented of the evil which he thought to have done, repentance was hidden from Saul, and therefore hidden from God's eyes.
entries.b3e6577d9720061d1007d074438df36ea9c87851: <div eID="gen5575" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Agag Slain. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1065.)</title> <div sID="gen5576" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">32</hi> Then said Samuel, Bring ye hither to me Agag the king of the Amalekites. And Agag came unto him delicately. And Agag said, Surely the bitterness of death is past. <hi type="super">33</hi> And Samuel said, As thy sword hath made women childless, so shall thy mother be childless among women. And Samuel hewed Agag in pieces before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> in Gilgal. <hi type="super">34</hi> Then Samuel went to Ramah; and Saul went up to his house to Gibeah of Saul. <hi type="super">35</hi> And Samuel came no more to see Saul until the day of his death: nevertheless Samuel mourned for Saul: and the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> repented that he had made Saul king over Israel. <div eID="gen5576" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5577" type="x-p"/> Samuel, as a prophet, is here set over kings, <reference osisRef="Jer.1.10">Jer. i. 10</reference>. <div eID="gen5577" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5578" type="x-p"/> I. He destroys king Agag, doubtless by such special direction from heaven as none now can pretend to. He <hi type="italic">hewed Agag in pieces.</hi> Some think he only ordered it to be done; or perhaps he did it with his own hands, as a sacrifice to God's injured justice (<reference osisRef="1Sam.15.33">v. 33</reference>), and sacrifices used to be cut in pieces. Now observe in this, <div eID="gen5578" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5579" type="x-p"/> 1. How Agag's present vain hopes were frustrated: He <hi type="italic">came delicately,</hi> in a stately manner, to show that he was a king, and therefore to be treated with respect, or in a soft effeminate manner, as one never used to hardship, that <hi type="italic">could not set the sole of his foot to the ground for tenderness and delicacy</hi> (<reference osisRef="Deut.28.56">Deut. xxviii. 56</reference>), to move compassion: and he said, "Surely, now that the heat of the battle is over, <hi type="italic">the bitterness of death is past,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.32">v. 32</reference>. Having escaped the sword of Saul," that man of war, he thought he was in no danger from Samuel, and old prophet, a man of peace. Note, (1.) There is bitterness in death, it is terrible to nature. <hi type="italic">Surely death is bitter,</hi> so divers versions read those words of Agag; as the LXX. read the former clause, <hi type="italic">He came trembling.</hi> Death will dismay the stoutest heart. (2.) Many think the bitterness of death is past when it is not so; they put that evil day far from them which is very near. True believers may, through grace, say this, upon good grounds, though death be not past, the bitterness of it is. <hi type="italic">O death! where is thy sting?</hi> <div eID="gen5579" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5580" type="x-p"/> 2. How his former wicked practices were now punished. Samuel calls him to account, not only for the sins of his ancestors, but his own sins: <hi type="italic">Thy sword has made women childless,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.33">v. 33</reference>. He trod in the steps of his ancestors' cruelty, and those under him, it is likely, did the same; justly therefore is all the righteous blood shed by Amalek required of this generation, <reference osisRef="Matt.23.36">Matt. xxiii. 36</reference>. Agag, that was delicate and luxurious himself, was cruel and barbarous to others. It is commonly so: those who are indulgent in their appetites are not less indulgent of their passions. But blood will be reckoned for; even kings must account to the King of kings for the guiltless blood they shed or cause to be shed. It was that crime of king Manasseh which the Lord would not pardon, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.4">2 Kings xxiv. 4</reference>. See <reference osisRef="Rev.13.10">Rev. xiii. 10</reference>. <div eID="gen5580" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5581" type="x-p"/> II. He deserts king Saul, takes leave of him (<reference osisRef="1Sam.15.34">v. 34</reference>), and <hi type="italic">never came any more to see him</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Sam.15.35">v. 35</reference>), to advise or assist him in any of his affairs, because Saul did not desire his company nor would he be advised by him. He looked upon him as rejected of God, and therefore he forsook him. Though he might sometimes see him accidentally (as <reference osisRef="1Sam.19.24">ch. xix. 24</reference>), yet he never came to see him out of kindness or respect. Yet he <hi type="italic">mourned for Saul,</hi> thinking it a very lamentable thing that a man who stood so fair for great things should ruin himself so foolishly. He mourned for the bad state of the country, to which Saul was likely to have been so great a blessing, but now would prove a curse and a plague. He mourned for his everlasting state, having no hopes of bringing him to repentance. When he wept for him, it is likely, he made supplication, but the Lord had <hi type="italic">repented that he had made Saul king,</hi> and resolved to undo that work of his, so that Samuel's prayers prevailed not for him. Observe, We must mourn for the rejection of sinners, 1. Though we withdraw from them, and dare not converse familiarly with them. Thus the prophet determines to leave his people and go from them, and yet to <hi type="italic">weep day and night for them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.9.1-Jer.9.2">Jer. ix. 1, 2</reference>. 2. Though they do not mourn for themselves. Saul seems unconcerned at the tokens of God's displeasure which he lay under, and yet Samuel mourns day and night for him. Jerusalem was secure when Christ wept over it.  <chapter eID="1Sam.15"/> <div eID="gen5581" type="x-p"/>

entries.91b42a41e83dba32c56bdcecc2aec77a02ef518c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2636"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 15</title> <div sID="gen3574" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.1-1Sam.15.6">1Sa 15:1-6</reference>. Saul Sent to Destroy Amalek.<div eID="gen3574" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3575" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2636"/><hi type="bold">1. Samuel also said unto Saul, The Lord sent me to anoint thee ...: now therefore hearken thou unto ... the Lord--</hi>Several years had been passed in successful military operations against troublesome neighbors. During these Saul had been left to act in a great measure at his own discretion as an independent prince. Now a second test is proposed of his possessing the character of a theocratic monarch in Israel; and in announcing the duty required of him, Samuel brought before him his official station as the Lord's vicegerent, and the peculiar obligation under which he was laid to act in that capacity. He had formerly done wrong, for which a severe rebuke and threatening were administered to him (<reference osisRef="1Sam.13.13">1Sa 13:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.13.14">14</reference>). Now an opportunity was afforded him of retrieving that error by an exact obedience to the divine command. <div eID="gen3575" type="x-p"/>
entries.f82af30b7a87bc9dd100cdfdce66ecccd3fa5a28: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2637"/><div sID="gen3576" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2637"/><hi type="bold">2-3. Amalek--</hi>the powerful tribe which inhabited the country immediately to the eastward of the northern Cushites. Their territory extended over the whole of the eastern portion of the desert of Sinai to Rephidim--the earliest opponent (<reference osisRef="Deut.25.18">De 25:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.17.8-Exod.17.16">Ex 17:8-16</reference>)--the hereditary and restless enemy of Israel (<reference osisRef="Num.14.45">Nu 14:45</reference>; <reference osisRef="Judg.3.13">Jud 3:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Judg.6.3">6:3</reference>), and who had not repented (<reference osisRef="1Sam.14.48">1Sa 14:48</reference>) of their bitter and sleepless hatred during the five hundred years that had elapsed since their doom was pronounced. Being a people of nomadic habits, they were as plundering and dangerous as the Bedouin Arabs, particularly to the southern tribes. The national interest required, and God, as King of Israel, decreed that this public enemy should be removed. Their destruction was to be without reservation or exception.<div eID="gen3576" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3577" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I remember--</hi>I am reminded of what Amalek did--perhaps by the still remaining trophy or memorial erected by Moses (<reference osisRef="Exod.17.15">Ex 17:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.17.16">16</reference>). <div eID="gen3577" type="x-p"/>
entries.f1981e38a05731a0cf159449bc2e997b62cb2aa6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2638"/><div sID="gen3578" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2638"/><hi type="bold">4. Saul gathered the people together--</hi>The alacrity with which he entered on the necessary preparations for the expedition gave a fair, but delusive promise of faithfulness in its execution.<div eID="gen3578" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3579" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Telaim--</hi>or Telem, among the uttermost cities of the tribe of Judah towards the coast of Edom (<reference osisRef="Josh.15.21">Jos 15:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Josh.15.24">24</reference>). <div eID="gen3579" type="x-p"/>
entries.d289ffa3501b58c3100812875f22fd4c6f1a1b75: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2639"/><div sID="gen3580" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2639"/><hi type="bold">5. Saul came to a city of Amalek--</hi>probably their capital.<div eID="gen3580" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3581" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">laid wait in the valley--</hi>following the strategic policy of Joshua at Ai (<reference osisRef="Josh.8.4">Jos 8:4</reference>). <div eID="gen3581" type="x-p"/>
entries.b56a4764947d5d022c6e41c5291b290fdde3b64e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2640"/><div sID="gen3582" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2640"/><hi type="bold">6. Kenites--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Judg.1.16">Jud 1:16</reference>). In consequence, probably, of the unsettled state of Judah, they seem to have returned to their old desert tracts. Though now intermingled with the Amalekites, they were not implicated in the offenses of that wicked race; but for the sake of their ancestors, between whom and those of Israel there had been a league of amity, a timely warning was afforded them to remove from the scene of danger.<div eID="gen3582" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3583" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.7-1Sam.15.9">1Sa 15:7-9</reference>. He Spares Agag and the Best of the Spoil. <div eID="gen3583" type="x-p"/>
entries.9eb7a6ebd47c2590c82f9b25e0157f034e94b138: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2641"/><div sID="gen3584" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2641"/><hi type="bold">7-9. Saul smote the Amalekites--</hi>His own view of the proper and expedient course to follow was his rule, not the command of God. <div eID="gen3584" type="x-p"/>
entries.ea1a66b84ea463b8c9f8bd9c87024722bd140a19: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2643"/><div sID="gen3587" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2643"/><hi type="bold">10-11. Then came the word of the Lord unto Samuel, saying, It repenteth me that I have set up Saul--</hi>Repentance is attributed in Scripture to Him when bad men give Him cause to alter His course and method of procedure, and to treat them as if He did "repent" of kindness shown. To the heart of a man like Samuel, who was above all envious considerations, and really attached to the king, so painful an announcement moved all his pity and led him to pass a sleepless night of earnest intercession. <div eID="gen3587" type="x-p"/>
entries.c76887f60cbb811e189d4be7a5870b10ae15591b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2644"/><div sID="gen3588" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2644"/><hi type="bold">12. Saul came to Carmel--</hi>in the south of Judah (<reference osisRef="Josh.15.55">Jos 15:55</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.2">1Sa 25:2</reference>).<div eID="gen3588" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3589" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he set him up a place--</hi>that is, a pillar (<reference osisRef="2Sam.18.18">2Sa 18:18</reference>); literally, a hand, indicating that whatever was the form of the monument, it was surmounted, according to the ancient fashion, by the figure of a hand, the symbol of power and energy. The erection of this vainglorious trophy was an additional act of disobedience. His pride had overborne his sense of duty in first raising this monument to his own honor, and then going to Gilgal to offer sacrifice to God. <div eID="gen3589" type="x-p"/>
entries.262641d33b349927bdf6daffe080e78c0ae60aa9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2645"/><div sID="gen3590" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2645"/><hi type="bold">13-23. Saul said unto him, Blessed be thou of the Lord: I have performed the commandment of the Lord--</hi>Saul was either blinded by a partial and delusive self-love, or he was, in his declaration to Samuel, acting the part of a bold and artful hypocrite. He professed to have fulfilled the divine command, and that the blame of any defects in the execution lay with the people. Samuel saw the real state of the case, and in discharge of the commission he had received before setting out, proceeded to denounce his conduct as characterized by pride, rebellion, and obstinate disobedience. When Saul persisted in declaring that he had obeyed, alleging that the animals, whose bleating was heard, had been reserved for a liberal sacrifice of thanksgiving to God, his shuffling, prevaricating answer called forth a stern rebuke from the prophet. It well deserved it--for the destination of the spoil to the altar was a flimsy pretext--a gross deception, an attempt to conceal the selfishness of the original motive under the cloak of religious zeal and gratitude. <div eID="gen3590" type="x-p"/>
entries.0982f4dcbbcd5bea71593796a0a226eb05091ded: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2646"/><div sID="gen3591" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2646"/><hi type="bold">24-26. I have sinned ... turn again with me, that I may worship the Lord--</hi>The erring, but proud and obstinate monarch was now humbled. He was conscience-smitten for the moment, but his confession proceeded not from sincere repentance, but from a sense of danger and desire of averting the sentence denounced against him. For the sake of public appearance, he besought Samuel not to allow their serious differences to transpire, but to join with him in a public act of worship. Under the influence of his painfully agitated feelings, he designed to offer sacrifice, partly to express his gratitude for the recent victory, and partly to implore mercy and a reversal of his doom. It was, from another angle, a politic scheme, that Samuel might be betrayed into a countenancing of his design in reserving the cattle for sacrificing. Samuel declined to accompany him.<div eID="gen3591" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3592" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I feared the people, and obeyed their voice--</hi>This was a different reason from the former he had assigned. It was the language of a man driven to extremities, and even had it been true, the principles expounded by Samuel showed that it could have been no extenuation of the offense. The prophet then pronounced the irreversible sentence of the rejection of Saul and his family. He was judicially cut off for his disobedience. <div eID="gen3592" type="x-p"/>
entries.745e13ea932278121f6984cd2454d724a5628bbe: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2647"/><div sID="gen3593" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2647"/><hi type="bold">27-28. he laid hold upon the skirt of his mantle--</hi>the moil, upper tunic, official robe. In an agony of mental excitement, he took hold of the prophet's dress to detain him; the rending of the mantle [1Sa 15:27] was adroitly pointed to as a significant and mystical representation of his severance from the throne. <div eID="gen3593" type="x-p"/>
entries.38c29cb37773c6bdf1492de2515831800828d6f9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2648"/><div sID="gen3594" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2648"/><hi type="bold">29. the Strength of Israel will not lie--</hi>Hebrew, "He that gives a victory to Israel," a further rebuke of his pride in rearing the Carmel trophy, and an intimation that no loss would be sustained in Israel by his rejection. <div eID="gen3594" type="x-p"/>
entries.7b1b0261b60921c2e45eb9724db491149424b810: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2649"/><div sID="gen3595" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2649"/><hi type="bold">31. Samuel turned again after Saul--</hi>not to worship along with him; but first, that the people might have no ground, on pretense of Saul's rejection, to withdraw their allegiance from him; and secondly, to compensate for Saul's error, by executing God's judgment upon Agag. <div eID="gen3595" type="x-p"/>
entries.abcf81760c9e784ad24186b56390abe31c354c9f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2650"/><div sID="gen3596" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2650"/><hi type="bold">32. Agag came unto him delicately--</hi>or cheerfully, since he had gained the favor and protection of the king. <div eID="gen3596" type="x-p"/>
entries.635a96a60e0311105ce75cb520e4e40edb747a7c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2651"/><div sID="gen3597" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2651"/><hi type="bold">33. Samuel hewed Agag--</hi>This cruel tyrant met the retribution of a righteous Providence. Never has it been unusual for great or official personages in the East to perform executions with their own hands. Samuel did it "before the Lord" in Gilgal, appointing that same mode of punishment (hitherto unknown in Israel) to be used towards him, which he had formerly used towards others. <chapter eID="1Sam.15"/>

entries.be58e1ef09c37f04ed5bfe1e16d2c7f510296655: <div eID="gen10085" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen10086" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen10087" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen10087" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen10086" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen10088" type="x-p"/> Samuel sends Saul to destroy the Amalekites, and all their substance, <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.1-1Sam.15.3">1Sam 15:1-3</reference>. Saul collects an immense army and comes against their city, <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.4">1Sam 15:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.5">1Sam 15:5</reference>. He desires the Kenites to remove from among the Amalekites, <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.6">1Sam 15:6</reference>. He smites the Amalekites, and takes their king, Agag, prisoner, and saves the best of the spoil, <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.7-1Sam.15.9">1Sam 15:7-9</reference>. The Lord is displeased, and sends Samuel to reprove him, <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.10">1Sam 15:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.11">1Sam 15:11</reference>. The conversation between Samuel and Saul, in which the latter endeavors to justify his conduct, <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.12-1Sam.15.23">1Sam 15:12-23</reference>. He is convinced that he has done wrong, and asks pardon, <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.24-1Sam.15.31">1Sam 15:24-31</reference>. Samuel causes Agag to be slain; for which he assigns the reasons, <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.32-1Sam.15.35">1Sam 15:32-35</reference>. <div eID="gen10088" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10089" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen10089" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10090" type="x-p"/> The Lord sent me to anoint thee - This gave him a right to say what immediately follows.
entries.836cd3d69aaca408fd6cde525e1e087c40c4139a: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen10090" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10091" type="x-p"/> I remember that which Amalek did - The Amalekites were a people of Arabia Petraea, who had occupied a tract of country on the frontiers of Egypt and Palestine. They had acted with great cruelty towards the Israelites on their coming out of Egypt. (See <reference osisRef="Exo.17.8">Exo 17:8</reference> (note), and the notes there). They came upon them when they were faint and weary, and smote the hindermost of the people - those who were too weak to keep up with the rest. (See <reference osisRef="Deu.25.18">Deu 25:18</reference>). And God then purposed that Amalek, as a nation, should be blotted out from under heaven; which purpose was now fulfilled by Saul upwards of four hundred years afterwards!
entries.c1f90043d5effff055b98a63cfcab01fbeafb1a5: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen10091" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10092" type="x-p"/> Slay both man and woman - Nothing could justify such an exterminating decree but the absolute authority of God. This was given: all the reasons of it we do not know; but this we know well, The Judge of all the earth doth right. This war was not for plunder, for God commanded that all the property as well as all the people should be destroyed.
entries.73ffd862b7bbe1f1d174ef7ccdcc20d0755bf71b: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen10092" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10093" type="x-p"/> Two hundred thousand - and ten thousand - The Septuagint, in the London Polyglot, have Four Hundred thousand companies of Israel, and Thirty thousand companies of Judah. The Codex Alexandrinus has Ten thousand of each. The Complutensian Polyglot has Two Hundred thousand companies of Israel, and Ten thousand of Judah. And Josephus has Four Hundred thousand of Israel, and Thirty thousand of Judah. All the other versions are the same with the Hebrew text; and there is no difference in the MSS.
entries.beee7812bf33dbeaaaaffb7d0785521bd564537d: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen10093" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10094" type="x-p"/> Saul came to a city of Amalek - I believe the original should be translated, and Saul came to the city Amalek; their capital being called by the name of their tribe.
entries.09c1b217cfe1ef9bc2e49bd0cf26992397d8f0e3: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen10094" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10095" type="x-p"/> Said unto the Kenites - The Kenites were an ancient people. Jethro, the father-in-law of Moses, was a Kenite. Hobab his son (if the same person be not meant) was guide to the Hebrews through the wilderness. They had a portion of the promised land, near to the city Arad. See <reference osisRef="Jdg.1.16">Jdg 1:16</reference>; and for more particulars concerning them and the Amalekites, see the notes on <reference osisRef="Num.26.20-Num.26.21">Num 26:20-21</reference> (note).
entries.fe4808a1a43b9dfb6ff737a37dcd1b9680d8ae03: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen10095" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10096" type="x-p"/> From Havilah - to Shur - From Pelusium in Egypt, unto the Red Sea. - Josephus. But Havilah lay eastward from the Red Sea; the Amalekites lay between this and the way to Egypt towards Shur.
entries.21d1975de8827c5446b447b625db64c63a64e0c5: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen10096" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10097" type="x-p"/> It repenteth me that I have set up Saul - That is, I placed him on the throne; I intended, if he had been obedient, to have established his kingdom. He has been disobedient; I change my purpose, and the kingdom shall not be established in his family. This is what is meant by God's repenting - changing a purpose according to conditions already laid down or mentally determined.
entries.4a76da203b5ec30172dc8bb3008b31cb2bbdc5b1: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen10097" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10098" type="x-p"/> He set him up a place - Literally, a hand, יד yad. Some say it was a monument; others, a triumphal arch: probably it was no more than a hand, pointing out the place where Saul had gained the victory. Absalom's pillar is called the hand of Absalom, <reference osisRef="2Sam.18.18">2Sam 18:18</reference>.
entries.59b247aec8074ca35f41a395595debff13b6a79e: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen10098" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10099" type="x-p"/> The people spared the best of the sheep - It is very likely that the people did spare the best of the prey; and it is as likely that Saul might have restrained them if he would. That they might not love war, God had interdicted spoil and plunder, so the war was undertaken merely from a sense of duty, without any hope of enriching themselves by it.
entries.ccaecad0f6ce61bdc635e94273bab41a0679c436: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen10099" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10100" type="x-p"/> Little in thine own sight - Who can bear prosperity? Is it not of the Lord's great goodness that the majority of the inhabitants of the earth are in comparative poverty?
entries.37371080ed21b45f1911e7f88fc02618c3719870: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen10100" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10101" type="x-p"/> To sacrifice unto the Lord - Thus he endeavors to excuse the people. They did not take the spoil in order to enrich themselves by it, but to sacrifice unto the Lord; and did not this motive justify their conduct?
entries.040f09e7395f35e6013459a1bd5d592bceefb48f: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen10101" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10102" type="x-p"/> Hath the Lord as great delight, etc. - This was a very proper answer to, and refutation of Saul's excuse. Is not obedience to the will of God the end of all religion, of its rites, ceremonies, and sacrifices?
entries.76ca4b1e03af4d93bd4ff75bb04425b272373724: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen10102" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10103" type="x-p"/> For rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft, and stubbornness is as iniquity and idolatry - This is no translation of those difficult words, כי חטאת קסם מרי ואון ותרפים הפצר ki chattath kesem meri veaven utheraphim haphtsar. It appears to me that the three nouns which occur first in the text refer each to the three last in order. Thus, חטאת chattath, Transgression, refers to און aven, Iniquity, which is the principle whence transgression springs. קסם kesem, Divination, refers to תרפים teraphim, consecrated images or telesms, vulgarly talismans, used in incantations. And מרי meri, Rebellion, refers evidently to הפצר haphstar, Stubbornness, whence rebellion springs. The meaning therefore of this difficult place may be the following: As transgression comes from iniquity, divination from teraphim, and rebellion from stubbornness, so, because thou hast rejected the word of the Lord, he hath also rejected thee from being king. All the versions are different.
entries.ec7c0e6296c2e048782e7e34e64386c5e1a7df37: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen10103" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10104" type="x-p"/> I have sinned - because I feared the people - This was the best excuse he could make for himself; but had he feared God more, he need have feared the People less.
entries.c05185abc626eba6d67aa83839138b24d141a39c: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen10104" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10105" type="x-p"/> Pardon my sin - Literally, bear my sin; take it away; forgive what I have done against thee, and be my intercessor with God, that he may forgive my offense against him; turn again with me, that I may worship the Lord.
entries.703fd6d9bb03f75c771413ed2693aa5200a0b5d9: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen10105" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10106" type="x-p"/> I will not return with thee - I cannot acknowledge thee as king, seeing the Lord hath rejected thee.
entries.ee3d449f3560000b114cd665231d9b2140dd85db: <hi type="bold">Verse 29</hi> <div eID="gen10106" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10107" type="x-p"/> The Strength of Israel will not lie - What God has purposed he will bring to pass, for he has all power in the heavens and in the earth; and he will not repent - change his purpose - concerning thee. <div eID="gen10107" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10108" type="x-p"/> We may say it was some extenuation of Saul's fault that the people insisted on preserving the best of the prey; for who could resist the demands of a victorious mob? But his crime was in consenting; had he not, the crime would have been theirs alone.
entries.3538b218a996a79754e20c31ec8d510017615ebd: <hi type="bold">Verse 32</hi> <div eID="gen10108" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10109" type="x-p"/> Agag came unto him delicately - The Septuagint have τρεμων, trembling; the original, מעדנת maadannoth, delicacies; probably איש ish, man, understood; a man of delights, a pleasure-taker: the Vulgate, pinguissimus et tremens, "very fat and trembling." <div eID="gen10109" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10110" type="x-p"/> Surely the bitterness of death is past - Almost all the versions render this differently from ours. Surely death is bitter, is their general sense; and this seems to be the true meaning.
entries.4a8dbcd300748cfa750efb3dac07db4e9fb92c13: <hi type="bold">Verse 33</hi> <div eID="gen10110" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10111" type="x-p"/> As thy sword hath made women childless - It appears that Agag had forfeited his life by his own personal transgressions, and that his death now was the retribution of his cruelties. <div eID="gen10111" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10112" type="x-p"/> And Samuel hewed Agag in pieces - <div eID="gen10112" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10113" type="x-p"/> 1. What Samuel did here he did in his magisterial capacity; and, <div eID="gen10113" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10114" type="x-p"/> 2. It is not likely he did it by his own sword, but by that of an executioner. What kings, magistrates, and generals do, in an official way, by their subjects, servants, or soldiers, they are said to do themselves; qui facit per alterum, facit per se.
entries.1b98f148322aebe82c06ec75a994096af7ea0740: <hi type="bold">Verse 35</hi> <div eID="gen10114" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10115" type="x-p"/> And Samuel came no more to see Saul - But we read, <reference osisRef="1Sam.19.22-1Sam.19.24">1Sam 19:22-24</reference>, that Saul went to see Samuel at Naioth, but this does not affect what is said here. From this time Samuel had no connection with Saul; he never more acknowledged him as king; he mourned and prayed for him, and continued to perform his prophetic functions at Ramah, and at Naioth, superintending the school of the prophets in that place.  <chapter eID="1Sam.15"/> <div eID="gen10115" type="x-p"/>

entries.5b09d8e946953c422c08b00c91837df9568d5fa9: <div eID="gen3890" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">War with Amalek. Saul’s Disobedience and Rejection - 1 Samuel 15</title> <div sID="gen3891" type="x-p"/> As Saul had transgressed the commandment of God which was given to him through Samuel, by the sacrifice which he offered at Gilgal in the war with the Philistines at the very commencement of his reign, and had thereby drawn upon himself the threat that his monarchy should not be continued in perpetuity (<reference osisRef="1Sam.13.13-1Sam.13.14">1Sa 13:13-14</reference>); so his disobedience in the war against the Amalekites was followed by his rejection on the part of God. The Amalekites were the first heathen nation to attack the Israelites after their deliverance out of Egypt, which they did in the most treacherous manner on their journey from Egypt to Sinai; and they had been threatened by God with extermination in consequence. This Moses enjoined upon Joshua, and also committed to writing, for the Israelites to observe in all future generations (<reference osisRef="Exod.17.8-Exod.17.16">Exo 17:8-16</reference>). As the Amalekites afterwards manifested the same hostility to the people of God which they had displayed in this first attack, on every occasion which appeared favourable to their ravages, the Lord instructed Samuel to issue the command to Saul, to wage war against Amalek, and to smite man and beast with the ban, i.e., to put all to death (<reference osisRef="1Sam.15.1-1Sam.15.3">1Sa 15:1-3</reference>). But when Saul had smitten them, he not only left Agag the king alive, but spared the best of the cattle that he had taken as booty, and merely executed the ban upon such animals as were worthless (<reference osisRef="1Sam.15.4-1Sam.15.9">1Sa 15:4-9</reference>). He was rejected by the Lord for this disobedience, so that he was to be no longer king over Israel. His rejection was announced to him by Samuel (<reference osisRef="1Sam.15.10-1Sam.15.23">1Sa 15:10-23</reference>), and was not retracted in spite of his prayer for the forgiveness of his sin (<reference osisRef="1Sam.15.24-1Sam.15.35">1Sa 15:24-35</reference>). In fact, Saul had no excuse for this breach of the divine command; it was nothing but open rebellion against the sovereignty of God in Israel; and if Jehovah would continue King of Israel, He must punish it by the rejection of the rebel. For Saul no longer desired to be the medium of the sovereignty of Jehovah, or the executor of the commands of the God-king, but simply wanted to reign according to his own arbitrary will. Nevertheless this rejection was not followed by his outward deposition. The Lord merely took away His Spirit, had David anointed king by Samuel, and thenceforward so directed the steps of Saul and David, that as time advanced the hearts of the people were turned away more and more from Saul to David; and on the death of Saul, the attempt of the ambitious Abner to raise his son Ishbosheth to the throne could not possibly have any lasting success. <div eID="gen3891" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3892" type="x-p"/> The account of the war against the Amalekites is a very condensed one, and is restricted to a description of the conduct of Saul on that occasion. Without mentioning either the time or the immediate occasion of the war, the narrative commences with the command of God which Samuel solemnly communicated to Saul, to go and exterminate that people. Samuel commenced with the words, “<hi type="italic">Jehovah sent me to anoint thee to be king over His people, over Israel</hi>,” in order to show to Saul the obligation which rested upon him to receive his commission as coming from God, and to proceed at once to fulfil it. The allusion to the anointing points back not to <reference osisRef="1Sam.11.15">1Sa 11:15</reference>, but to 1Sa 10:1.
entries.48d890ad2fcd4b65c4c2f46e9caeac4730e2254e: <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.2">1Sa 15:2</reference> <div eID="gen3892" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3893" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">Thus saith the Lord of Zebaoth, I have looked upon what Amalek did to Israel, that it placed itself in his way when he came up out of Egypt</hi>” (<reference osisRef="Exod.17.8">Exo 17:8</reference>). Samuel merely mentions this first outbreak of hostility on the part of Amalek towards the people of Israel, because in this the same disposition was already manifested which now made the people ripe for the judgment of extermination (vid., <reference osisRef="Exod.17.14">Exo 17:14</reference>). The hostility which they had now displayed, according to <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.33">1Sa 15:33</reference>, there was no necessity for the prophet to mention particularly, since it was well known to Saul and all Israel. When God looks upon a sin, directs His glance towards it, He must punish it according to His own holiness. This פּקדתּי points at the very outset to the punishment about to be proclaimed.
entries.552414f624befe6a95b36294543e2540fd16492d: <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.3">1Sa 15:3</reference> <div eID="gen3893" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3894" type="x-p"/> Saul is to smite and ban everything belonging to it without reserve, i.e., to put to death both man and beast. The last clause וגו is only an explanation and exemplification of וגו והחרמתּם. “<hi type="italic">From man to woman</hi>,” etc., i.e., men and women, children and sucklings, etc. <div eID="gen3894" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3895" type="x-p"/> Saul summoned the people to war, and mustered them (those who were summoned) at <hi type="italic">Telaim</hi> (this was probably the same place as the <hi type="italic">Telem</hi> mentioned in <reference osisRef="Josh.15.24">Jos 15:24</reference>, and is to be looked for in the eastern portion of the Negeb). “<hi type="italic">Two hundred thousand foot, and ten thousand of the men of Judah</hi>:” this implies that the two hundred thousand were from the other tribes. These numbers are not too large; for a powerful Bedouin nation, such as the Amalekites were, could not possibly be successfully attacked with a small army, but only by raising the whole of the military force of Israel.
entries.a22a62c9a1e31bdf77ec5d7f7ebbdcaaee4667f9: <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.5">1Sa 15:5</reference> <div eID="gen3895" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3896" type="x-p"/> He then advanced as far as the city of the Amalekites, the situation of which is altogether unknown, and placed an ambush in the valley. ויּרב does not come from ריב, to fight, i.e., to quarrel, not to give battle, but was understood even by the early translators as a contracted form of ויּארב, the <hi type="italic">Hiphil</hi> of ארב. And modern commentators have generally understood it in the same way; but Olshausen (<hi type="italic">Hebr.
