Gramm</hi>. p. 572) questions the correctness of the reading, and Thenius proposes to alter בּנּחל ויּרב into מלחמה ויּערך. נחל refers to a valley in the neighbourhood of the city of the Amalekites.
entries.aa077f3e2a23a1f3b94fcebad69dd56e6daf4dd4: <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.6-1Sam.15.7">1Sa 15:6-7</reference> <div eID="gen3896" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3897" type="x-p"/> Saul directed the Kenites to come out from among the Amalekites, that they might not perish with them (אספך, <hi type="italic">imp. Kal</hi> of אסף), as they had shown affection to the Israelites on their journey out of Egypt (compare Num 10:29 with Jdg 1:16). He then smote the Amalekites from Havilah in the direction towards Shur, which lay before (to the east of) Egypt (cf. <reference osisRef="Gen.25.18">Gen 25:18</reference>). <hi type="italic">Shur</hi> is the desert of Jifar, i.e., that portion of the desert of Arabia which borders upon Egypt (see at <reference osisRef="Gen.16.7">Gen 16:7</reference>). <hi type="italic">Havilah</hi>, the country of the <hi type="italic">Chaulotaeans</hi>, on the border of Arabia Petraea towards Yemen (see at <reference osisRef="Gen.10.29">Gen 10:29</reference>).
entries.cd90dc6cc0e5b5c57f4512e91fad2ea527a404d4: <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.8-1Sam.15.9">1Sa 15:8-9</reference> <div eID="gen3897" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3898" type="x-p"/> Their king, <hi type="italic">Agag</hi>, he took alive (on the name, see at Num 24:7), but all the people he banned with the edge of the sword, i.e., he had them put to death without quarter. “<hi type="italic">All</hi>,” i.e., all that fell into the hands of the Israelites. For it follows from the very nature of the case that many escaped, and consequently there is nothing striking in the fact that Amalekites are mentioned again at a later period (<reference osisRef="1Sam.27.8">1Sa 27:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.30.1">1Sa 30:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.12">2Sa 8:12</reference>). The last remnant was destroyed by the Simeonites upon the mountains of Seir in the reign of Hezekiah (<reference osisRef="1Chr.4.43">1Ch 4:43</reference>). Only, king Agag did Saul and the people (of Israel) spare, also “<hi type="italic">the best of the sheep and oxen, and the animals of the second birth, and the lambs and everything good; these they would not ban</hi>.” משׁנים, according to D. Kimchi and R. Tanch. , are לבטן שׁניים, i.e., <hi type="italic">animalia secundo partu edita</hi>, which were considered superior to the others (vid., <hi type="italic">Roediger</hi> in <hi type="italic">Ges. Thes</hi>. p. 1451); and כּרים, pasture lambs, i.e., fat lambs. There is no necessity, therefore, for the conjecture of <hi type="italic">Ewald</hi> and Thenius, משׁמנּים, fattened, and כּרמים, vineyards; nor for the far-fetched explanation given by Bochart, viz., camels with two humps and camel-saddles, to say nothing of the fact that camel-saddles and vineyards are altogether out of place here. In “<hi type="italic">all that was good</hi>” the things already mentioned singly are all included. המּלאכה, the property; here it is applied to cattle, as in Gen 33:14. נמבזה = נבזה, despised, undervalued. The form of the word is not contracted from a noun מבזה and the participle נבזה (<hi type="italic">Ges. Lehrgeb</hi>. p. 463), but seems to be a <hi type="italic">participle Niph</hi>. formed from a noun מבזה. But as such a form is contrary to all analogy, <hi type="italic">Ewald</hi> and Olshausen regard the reading as corrupt. נמס (from מסס): flowing away; used with reference to diseased cattle, or such as have perished. The reason for sparing the best cattle is very apparent, namely selfishness. But it is not so easy to determine why Agag should have been spared by Saul. It is by no means probable that he wished thereby to do honour to the royal dignity. <hi type="italic">O. v. Gerlach</hi>'s supposition, that vanity or the desire to make a display with a royal slave was the actual reason, is a much more probable one.
entries.9d8dc3c57d03025ea42568794e84c71ed377b49f: <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.10-1Sam.15.11">1Sa 15:10-11</reference> <div eID="gen3898" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3899" type="x-p"/> The word of the Lord came to Samuel: “<hi type="italic">It repenteth me that I have made Saul king, for he hath turned away from me, and not set up</hi> (carried out) <hi type="italic">my word</hi>.” (On the repentance of God, see the remarks on Gen 6:6.) That this does not express any changeableness in the divine nature, but simply the sorrow of the divine love at the rebellion of sinners, is evident enough from 1Sa 15:29. יי מאחרי שׁוּב, to turn round from following God, in order to go his own ways. This was Saul’s real sin. He would no longer be the follower and servant of the Lord, but would be absolute ruler in Israel. Pride arising from the consciousness of his own strength, led him astray to break the command of God. What more God said to Samuel is not communicated here, because it could easily be gathered and supplied from what Samuel himself proceeded to do (see more particularly 1Sa 15:16.). In order to avoid repetitions, only the principal feature in the divine revelation is mentioned here, and the details are given fully afterwards in the account of the fulfilment of the instructions. Samuel was deeply agitated by this word of the Lord. “<hi type="italic">It burned</hi> (in) <hi type="italic">him</hi>,” sc., wrath (אף, compare <reference osisRef="Gen.31.36">Gen 31:36</reference> with <reference osisRef="Gen.30.2">Gen 30:2</reference>), not on account of the repentance to which God had given utterance at having raised up Saul as king, nor merely at Saul’s disobedience, but at the frustration of the purpose of God in calling him to be king in consequence of his disobedience, from which he might justly dread the worst results in relation to the glory of Jehovah and his own prophetic labours.<note placement="foot">“Many grave thoughts seem to have presented themselves at once to Samuel and disturbed his mind, when he reflected upon the dishonour which might be heaped upon the name of God, and the occasion which the rejection and deposition of Saul would furnish to wicked men for blaspheming God. For Saul had been anointed by the ministry of Samuel, and he had been chosen by God himself from all the people, and called by Him to the throne. If, therefore, he was nevertheless deposed, it seemed likely that so much would be detracted from the authority of Samuel and the confidence of the people in his teaching, and, moreover, that the worship of God would be overturned, and the greatest disturbance ensue; in fact, that universal confusion would burst upon the nation. These were probably the grounds upon which Samuel’s great indignation rested.” - <hi type="italic">Calvin</hi>.</note> <div eID="gen3899" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3900" type="x-p"/> The opinion that ל יחר is also used to signify deep distress cannot be established from 2Sa 4:8. “<hi type="italic">And he cried to Jehovah the whole night</hi>,” sc., praying for Saul to be forgiven. But it was in vain. This is evident from what follows, where Samuel maintains the cause of his God with strength and decision, after having wrestled with God in prayer.
entries.eb93100cc6ca0c5478f2a084ded3ac90381eac16: <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.12">1Sa 15:12</reference> <div eID="gen3900" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3901" type="x-p"/> The next morning, after receiving the revelation from God (<reference osisRef="1Sam.15.11">1Sa 15:11</reference>), Samuel rose up early, to go and meet Saul as he was returning from the war. On the way it was told him, “<hi type="italic">Saul has come to Carmel</hi>” - i.e., <hi type="italic">Kurmul</hi>, upon the mountains of Judah to the south-east of Hebron (see at <reference osisRef="Josh.15.55">Jos 15:55</reference>) - “<hi type="italic">setting himself a memorial</hi>” (יד, a hand, then a memorial or monument, inasmuch as the hand calls attention to anything: see <reference osisRef="2Sam.18.18">2Sa 18:18</reference>), “<hi type="italic">and has turned and proceeded farther, and gone down to Gilgal</hi>” (in the valley of the Jordan, as in <reference osisRef="1Sam.13.4">1Sa 13:4</reference>).
entries.cf7193cd7104b4bb22b2557325d09b5b08b4fe2d: <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.13">1Sa 15:13</reference> <div eID="gen3901" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3902" type="x-p"/> When Samuel met him there, Saul attempted to hide his consciousness of guilt by a feigned friendly welcome. “<hi type="italic">Blessed be thou of the Lord</hi>” (vid., Rth 2:20; <reference osisRef="Gen.14.19">Gen 14:19</reference>, etc.) was his greeting to the prophet; “<hi type="italic">I have set up the word of Jehovah</hi>.”
entries.46aeb21d33221e95296932f35f2823369df5898a: <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.14-1Sam.15.15">1Sa 15:14-15</reference> <div eID="gen3902" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3903" type="x-p"/> But the prophet stripped his hypocrisy at once with the question, “<hi type="italic">What then is this bleating of sheep in my ears, and a lowing of oxen that I hear?</hi>” Saul replied (<reference osisRef="1Sam.15.15">1Sa 15:15</reference>), “<hi type="italic">They have brought them from the Amalekites, because the people spared the best sheep and oxen, to sacrifice them to the Lord thy God; and the rest we have banned</hi>.” So that it was not Saul, but the people, who had transgressed the command of the Lord, and that with the most laudable intention, viz., to offer the best of the cattle that had been taken, as a thank-offering to the Lord. The falsehood and hypocrisy of these words lay upon the very surface; for even if the cattle spared were really intended as sacrifices to the Lord, not only the people, but Saul also, would have had their own interests in view (vid., <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.9">1Sa 15:9</reference>), since the flesh of thank-offerings was appropriated to sacrificial meals.
entries.a48d641b99825882f235f187d04c3f0fae60e22f: <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.16-1Sam.15.19">1Sa 15:16-19</reference> <div eID="gen3903" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3904" type="x-p"/> Samuel therefore bade him be silent. הרף, “<hi type="italic">leave off</hi>,” excusing thyself any further. “<hi type="italic">I will tell thee what Jehovah hath said to me this night</hi>.” (The <hi type="italic">Chethibh</hi> ויּאמרוּ is evidently a copyist’s error for ויּאמר.) “<hi type="italic">Is it not true, when thou wast little in thine eyes</hi> (a reference to Saul’s own words, <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.21">1Sa 9:21</reference>), <hi type="italic">thou didst become head of the tribes of Israel? and Jehovah anointed thee king over Israel, and Jehovah sent thee on the way, and said, Go and ban the sinners, the Amalekites, and make war against them, until thou exterminatest them. And wherefore hast thou nor hearkened to the voice of Jehovah, and hast fallen upon the booty</hi>,” etc.? (תּעט, see at 1Sa 14:32.) <div eID="gen3904" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3905" type="x-p"/> Even after this Saul wanted to justify himself, and to throw the blame of sparing the cattle upon the people.
entries.eb94298e3dd3a68b564673b60f9b1ce0f3eaa189: <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.20">1Sa 15:20</reference> <div eID="gen3905" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3906" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">Yea, I have hearkened to the voice of Jehovah</hi> (אשׁר serving, like כּי ekil , to introduce the reply: here it is used in the sense of asseveration, <hi type="italic">utique</hi>, yea), <hi type="italic">and have brought Agag the king of the Amalekites, and banned Amalek</hi>.” Bringing Agag he mentioned probably as a practical proof that he had carried out the war of extermination against the Amalekites.
entries.1f17500daaf1b25cd15d3bd9118be290a6351b8c: <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.21">1Sa 15:21</reference> <div eID="gen3906" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3907" type="x-p"/> Even the sparing of the cattle he endeavoured to defend as the fulfilment of a religious duty. The people had taken sheep and oxen from the booty, “<hi type="italic">as firstlings of the ban</hi>,” to sacrifice to Jehovah. Sacrificing the best of the booty taken in war as an offering of first-fruits to the Lord, was not indeed prescribed in the law, but was a praiseworthy sign of piety, by which all honour was rendered to the Lord as the giver of the victory (see Num 31:48.). This, Saul meant to say, was what the people had done on the present occasion; only he overlooked the fact, that what was banned to the Lord could not be offered to Him as a burnt-offering, because, being most holy, it belonged to Him already (<reference osisRef="Lev.27.29">Lev 27:29</reference>), and according to <reference osisRef="Deut.13.16">Deu 13:16</reference>, was to be put to death, as Samuel had expressly said to Saul (<reference osisRef="1Sam.15.3">1Sa 15:3</reference>).
entries.e43a50c73c068ec47afb557898185d237f278211: <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.22-1Sam.15.23">1Sa 15:22-23</reference> <div eID="gen3907" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3908" type="x-p"/> Without entering, therefore, into any discussion of the meaning of the ban, as Saul only wanted to cover over his own wrong-doings by giving this turn to the affair, Samuel put a stop to any further excuses, by saying, “<hi type="italic">Hath Jehovah delight in burnt-offerings and slain-offerings as in hearkening to the voice of Jehovah?</hi> (i.e., in obedience to His word.) <hi type="italic">Behold, hearing</hi> (obeying) <hi type="italic">is better than slain-offerings, attending better than fat of rams</hi>.” By saying this, Samuel did not reject sacrifices as worthless; he did not say that God took no pleasure in burnt-offerings and slain-offerings, but simply compared sacrifice with obedience to the command of God, and pronounced the latter of greater worth than the former. “It was as much as to say that the sum and substance of divine worship consisted in obedience, with which it should always begin, and that sacrifices were, so to speak, simple appendices, the force and worth of which were not so great as of obedience to the precepts of God” (Calvin). But it necessarily follows that sacrifices without obedience to the commandments of God are utterly worthless; in fact, are displeasing to God, as Psa 50:8., Isa 1:11., <reference osisRef="Isa.66.3">Isa 66:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.6.20">Jer 6:20</reference>, and all the prophets, distinctly affirm. There was no necessity, however, to carry out this truth any further. To tear off the cloak of hypocrisy, with which Saul hoped to cover his disobedience, it was quite enough to affirm that God’s first demand was obedience, and that observing His word was better than sacrifice; because, as the <hi type="italic">Berleb. Bible</hi> puts it, “in sacrifices a man offers only the strange flesh of irrational animals, whereas in obedience he offers his own will, which is rational or spiritual worship” (<reference osisRef="Rom.12.8">Rom 12:8</reference>). This spiritual worship was shadowed forth in the sacrificial worship of the Old Testament. In the sacrificial animal the Israelite was to give up and sanctify his own person and life to the Lord. (For an examination of the meaning of the different sacrifices, see <hi type="italic">Pent</hi>. pp. 505ff., and Keil’s <hi type="italic">Bibl Archäol</hi>. §41ff.) But if this were the design of the sacrifices, it was clear enough that God did not desire the animal sacrifice in itself, but first and chiefly obedience to His own word. In <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.22">1Sa 15:22</reference>, טּוב is not to be connected as an adjective with זבח, “more than good sacrifice,” as the <hi type="italic">Sept.</hi> and Thenius render it; it is rather to be taken as a predicate, “<hi type="italic">better than slain-offerings</hi>,” and מזּבח is placed first simply for the sake of emphasis. Any contrast between good and bad sacrifices, such as the former construction would introduce into the words, is not only foreign to the context, but also opposed to the parallelism. For אילים חלב does not mean fat rams, but the fat of rams; the fat portions taken from the ram, which were placed upon the altar in the case of the slain-offerings, and for which חלב is the technical expression (compare <reference osisRef="Lev.3.9">Lev 3:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.3.16">Lev 3:16</reference>, with <reference osisRef="Lev.3.4">Lev 3:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.3.11">Lev 3:11</reference>, etc.). “<hi type="italic">For</hi>,” continued Samuel (<reference osisRef="1Sam.15.23">1Sa 15:23</reference>), “<hi type="italic">rebellion is the sin of soothsaying, and opposition is heathenism and idolatry</hi>.” מרי and הפצר are the subjects, and synonymous in their meaning. קסם חטּאת, the sin of soothsaying, i.e., of divination in connection with the worship of idolatrous and demoniacal powers. In the second clause idols are mentioned instead of idolatry, and compared to resistance, but without any particle of comparison. Opposition is keeping idols and teraphim, i.e., it is like worshipping idols and teraphim. און, nothingness, then an idol or image (vid., <reference osisRef="Isa.66.3">Isa 66:3</reference>; Hos 4:15; Hos 10:5, Hos 10:8). On the <hi type="italic">teraphim</hi> as domestic and oracular deities, see at Gen 31:19. Opposition to God is compared by Samuel to soothsaying and oracles, because idolatry was manifested in both of them. All conscious disobedience is actually idolatry, because it makes self-will, the human I, into a god. So that all manifest opposition to the word and commandment of God is, like idolatry, a rejection of the true God. “<hi type="italic">Because thou hast rejected the word of Jehovah, He hath rejected thee, that thou mayst be no longer king</hi>.” ממּלך = מלך מהיוה (<reference osisRef="1Sam.15.26">1Sa 15:26</reference>), away from being king.
entries.8daac6a02a9afcbe0b45d9487802a1d29e299cd7: <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.24-1Sam.15.25">1Sa 15:24-25</reference> <div eID="gen3908" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3909" type="x-p"/> This sentence made so powerful an impression upon Saul, that he confessed, “<hi type="italic">I have sinned: for I have transgressed the command of the Lord and thy words, because I feared the people, and hearkened to their voice</hi>.” But these last words, with which he endeavoured to make his sin appear as small as possible, show that the consciousness of his guilt did not go very deep. Even if the people had really desired that the best of the cattle should be spared, he ought not as king to have given his consent to their wish, since God had commanded that they should all be banned (i.e., destroyed); and even though he has yielded from weakness, this weakness could not lessen his guilt before God. This repentance, therefore, was rather the effect of alarm at the rejection which had been announced to him, than the fruit of any genuine consciousness of sin. “It was not true and serious repentance, or the result of genuine sorrow of heart because he had offended God, but was merely repentance of the lips arising from fear of losing the kingdom, and of incurring public disgrace” (C. v. Lapide). This is apparent even from <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.25">1Sa 15:25</reference>, but still more from 1Sa 15:30. In <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.25">1Sa 15:25</reference> he not only entreats Samuel for the forgiveness of his sin, but says, “<hi type="italic">Return with me, that I may pray to the Lord</hi>.” The שׁוּב presupposes that Samuel was about to go away after the executing his commission. Saul entreated him to remain that he might pray, i.e., not only in order to obtain for him the forgiveness of his sin through his intercession, but, according to <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.30">1Sa 15:30</reference>, to show him honour before the elders of the people and before Israel, that his rejection might not be known.
entries.b03da468d5c7b0429ab487a9b9e2696f7d34f5b3: <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.26-1Sam.15.29">1Sa 15:26-29</reference> <div eID="gen3909" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3910" type="x-p"/> This request Samuel refused, repeating at the same time the sentence of rejection, and turned to depart. “<hi type="italic">Then Saul laid hold of the lappet of his mantle</hi> (i.e., his upper garment), <hi type="italic">and it tore</hi>” (<hi type="italic">lit</hi>. was torn off). That the <hi type="italic">Niphal</hi> ויּקּרע is correct, and is not to be altered into אתהּ ויּקרע, “Saul tore off the lappet,” according to the rendering of the lxx, as Thenius supposes, is evident from the explanation which Samuel gave of the occurrence (<reference osisRef="1Sam.15.28">1Sa 15:28</reference>): “<hi type="italic">Jehovah hath torn the sovereignty of Israel from thee to-day, and given it to thy neighbour, who is better than thou</hi>.” As Saul was about to hold back the prophet by force, that he might obtain from him a revocation of the divine sentence, the tearing of the mantle, which took place accidentally, and evidently without any such intention on the part of Saul, was to serve as a sign of the rending away of the sovereignty from him. Samuel did not yet know to whom Jehovah would give it; he therefore used the expression לרעך, as רע is applied to any one with whom a person associates. To confirm his own words, he adds in <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.29">1Sa 15:29</reference> : “<hi type="italic">And also the Trust of Israel doth not lie and doth not repent, for He is not a man to repent</hi>.” נצח signifies constancy, endurance, then confidence, trust, because a man can trust in what is constant. This meaning is to be retained here, where the word is used as a name for God, and not the meaning <hi type="italic">gloria</hi>, which is taken in <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.11">1Ch 29:11</reference> from the Aramaean usage of speech, and would be altogether unsuitable here, where the context suggests the idea of unchangeableness. For a man’s repentance or regret arises from his changeableness, from the fluctuations in his desires and actions. This is never the case with God; consequently He is ישׂראל נצח, <hi type="italic">the unchangeable One, in whom Israel can trust, since He does not lie or deceive, or repent of His purposes</hi>. These words are spoken θεοπρεπῶς (theomorphically), whereas in <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.11">1Sa 15:11</reference> and other passages, which speak of God as repenting, the words are to be understood ἀνθρωποπαθῶς (anthropomorphically; cf. Num 23:19).
entries.d50a3917ec0af5eccb14a5a53addf91f44e8baca: <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.30-1Sam.15.31">1Sa 15:30-31</reference> <div eID="gen3910" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3911" type="x-p"/> After this declaration as to the irrevocable character of the determination of God to reject Saul, Samuel yielded to the renewed entreaty of Saul, that he would honour him by his presence before the elders and the people, and remained whilst Saul worshipped, not merely “for the purpose of preserving the outward order until a new king should take his place” (<hi type="italic">O. v. Gerlach</hi>), but also to carry out the ban upon Agag, whom Saul had spared.
entries.9f07559f09b0ca5c5ce40b66e6b0760922127a25: <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.32">1Sa 15:32</reference> <div eID="gen3911" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3912" type="x-p"/> After Saul had prayed, Samuel directed him to bring Agag the king of the Amalekites. Agag came מעדנּת, i.e., in a contented and joyous state of mind, and said (in his heart), “<hi type="italic">Surely the bitterness of death is vanished</hi>,” not from any special pleasure at the thought of death, or from a heroic contempt of death, but because he thought that his life was to be granted him, as he had not been put to death at once, and was now about to be presented to the prophet (Clericus).
entries.72492e377adb0192218e245db76a9bddbf3073c6: <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.33">1Sa 15:33</reference> <div eID="gen3912" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3913" type="x-p"/> But Samuel pronounced the sentence of death upon him: “<hi type="italic">As thy sword hath made women childless, so be thy mother childless before women!</hi>” מנּשׁים is to be understood as a comparative: more childless than (other) women, i.e., the most childless of women, namely, because her son was the king. From these words of Samuel, it is very evident that Agag had carried on his wars with great cruelty, and had therefore forfeited his life according to the <hi type="italic">lex talionis</hi>. Samuel then hewed him in pieces “<hi type="italic">before the Lord at Gilgal</hi>,” i.e., before the altar of Jehovah there; for the slaying of Agag being the execution of the ban, was an act performed for the glory of God.
entries.4c0986b41f496d1e1de9a12955fa458aabc03943: <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.34-1Sam.15.35">1Sa 15:34-35</reference> <div eID="gen3913" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3914" type="x-p"/> After the prophet had thus maintained the rights of Jehovah in the presence of Saul, and carried out the ban upon Agag, he returned to his own home at Ramah; and Saul went to his house at Gibeah. From that time forward Samuel broke off all intercourse with the king whom Jehovah had rejected. “<hi type="italic">For Samuel was grieved for Saul, and it repented the Lord that he had made Saul king</hi>,” i.e., because Samuel had loved Saul on account of his previous election; and yet, as Jehovah had rejected him unconditionally, he felt that he was precluded from doing anything to effect a change of heart in Saul, and his reinstatement as king.  <chapter eID="1Sam.15"/> <div eID="gen3914" type="x-p"/>

                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Hath pronounced the Sentence of Rejection: for that he was not actually Rejected or Deposed by God, plainly appears, be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cause not onely the People, but even <ns0:hi>David,</ns0:hi> after this, own<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed him as King; and <ns0:hi>Samuel,</ns0:hi> at <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi>'s desire, did honour him; <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> own him as King, before the People, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 30.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="24">24 ¶ And Saul said unto Samuel, I have sin<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ned <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Which confession proceeded not from true Repentance, but from the sence of his great Danger, and from a desire of recalling that dreadful Sentence denounced against him.</ns0:note>: for I have transgressed the commandment of the LORD, and thy words <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> The Commandment of the Lord delivered to me by thy words. Another <ns0:hi>Hendiadis.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>; because I feared the people <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Who, as thou knowest, are set upon mischief, and would probably have broken forth into a Mutiny or Rebellion, had I done otherwise. But how little he feared the People, may be seen by 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 11. 7. and 14. 24. But this was a false cause: nor doth he acknow<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ledge the true cause, which was his Covetousness, and be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cause he did not fear God.</ns0:note>, and obeyed their voice.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="25">25 Now therefore, I pray thee, pardon my sin <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Use thy great Interest with God to obtain the Pardon of my sin. Or, do thou Pardon my sin against thee: for he had sinned not onely against God, but against <ns0:hi>Samuel</ns0:hi> also, as Gods Prophet; and therefore needed a Pardon both from God and Man.</ns0:note>, and turn again with me <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">To <ns0:hi>Gilgal,</ns0:hi> whence <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi> was gone forth to meet <ns0:hi>Samuel;</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Samuel</ns0:hi> is here said to turn again to <ns0:hi>Gil<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gal;</ns0:hi> not properly, for he had not now been there: but by way of Concomitancy, because he accompanied <ns0:hi>Saul,</ns0:hi> who was come thence, and returned thither: See the like expressi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on <ns0:hi>Ruth</ns0:hi> 1. 10, 22. and 2. 6.</ns0:note>, that I may wor<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ship the LORD <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">That I may offer further Sacrifices to God; partly, to Praise him for the past Victory; and partly, to Implore his Mercy, and the taking off of my sin and punishment. This was a politick device of <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi>'s; That <ns0:hi>Samuel</ns0:hi> might at least seem to countenance his Design, in reserving the Cattel for Sacrifice: which <ns0:hi>Samuel</ns0:hi> seeing, refused to do it. Heb. <ns0:hi>and I will worship the Lord;</ns0:hi> i. e. I will seek his Pardon and Favour.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="26">26 And Samuel said unto Saul, I will not re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />turn with thee <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">This was no lye, though he afterwards returned, because he spoke what he meant, his words and intentions agreed to<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gether, though afterwards he saw reason to change his in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tentions. Compare <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 19. 2, 3. Which may relieve many perplexed Consciences, who think themselves obliged to do what they have said they would do, though they see just cause to change their minds.</ns0:note>: for thou hast rejected the word of the LORD, and the LORD hath rejected thee from being king over Israel.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="27">27 And as Samuel turned about to go away, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">See 1 King. 11. 30.</ns0:note> he laid hold upon the skirt of his mantle, and it rent.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="28">28 And Samuel said unto him, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 28. 17. 1 King. 11. 3<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note> The LORD hath rent the kingdom of Israel from thee <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>Samuel</ns0:hi> makes use of the emergent occasion, as a sign, to signify and confirm his former Prediction.</ns0:note> this day, and hath given it to a neighbour of thine <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Either, a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nother Man: or, another <ns0:hi>Israelite:</ns0:hi> for the word <ns0:hi>Neighbour,</ns0:hi> is used both ways: or rather, one of a Neighbouring Tribe, even <ns0:hi>Iudah,</ns0:hi> whose Inheritance did not onely joyn to that of <ns0:hi>Ben<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />jamin,</ns0:hi> but was partly mixed with it.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>that is</ns0:hi> better than thou.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="29">29 And also the <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> eternity, or, victory.</ns0:note> strength of Israel <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">So he calls God here; partly, to shew the reason why God neither will nor can lye; because lying is a weakness, and proceeds from the sence of a Mans weakness, because he cannot many times accomplish his Design without lying and dissimulation; which therefore many Princes have used for this very reason. But, saith he, God needs no such Artifices; he can do whatsoever he pleaseth by his Absolute Power, and hath no need to use lyes to accomplish his Will: partly, to shew that <ns0:hi>Israel</ns0:hi> should be no loser by <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi>'s loss, as he might vainly imagine, because he had saved them from their Ene<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mies on every side, <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 14. 47. For not <ns0:hi>Saul,</ns0:hi> but God, was the Strength and Protector of <ns0:hi>Israel,</ns0:hi> and he would con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tinue to save them when <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi> was lost and gone: and part<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly, to assure <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi> that God would Execute this Threatning, because he wanted not strength to do it, and none could hinder him in it.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Num. 23. 19. 2 Tim. 2. 1<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>. Tit. 1. 2.</ns0:note> will not lie <ns0:hi>k,</ns0:hi> nor repent <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Nor ehange his Counsel; which also is an effect of weakness and imperfection, either of Wisdom or Power.</ns0:note>: for he <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> not a man that he should repent.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="30">30 Then he said, I have sinned; <ns0:hi>yet</ns0:hi> honour me now, I pray thee, before the elders of my people, and before Israel <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Here <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>e plainly discovers his Hypocrisie, and the true motive of this and his former Confession; he was not soli<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />citous for the Favour of God, but for his Honour and Power with <ns0:hi>Israel.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>, and turn again with me, that I may worship the LORD thy God.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="31">31 So Samuel turned again after Saul <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Not to Worship the Lord with him, for that he did not; and therefore it is here mentioned that <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi> onely <ns0:hi>Worshipped the Lord:</ns0:hi> but for two other reasons; First, That the Peo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ple might not upon pretence of this Sentence of rejection, immediately withdraw all Respect and Obedience to their Sovereign; whereby they would both have sinned against God, and have been as Sheep without a Shepherd. Second<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly, That he might rectify <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi>'s Error, and execute Gods Judgment upon <ns0:hi>Agag.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>, and Saul worshipped the LORD.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="32">32 ¶ Then said Samuel, Bring ye hither to me Agag the king <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> of Amalek.</ns0:note> of the Amalekites: and Agag came unto him delicately <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>in Delights;</ns0:hi> or, <ns0:hi>in his Ornaments;</ns0:hi> i. e. And Agag said <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>for</ns0:hi> Agag <ns0:hi>said:</ns0:hi> This being the reason why he came so.</ns0:note>, Surely the bitterness of death is past <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">I who have escaped Death from the hands of a Warlike Prince in the fury of Battel, shall certainly never suffer Death from an old Prophet in time of Peace.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="33">33 And Samuel said, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Num. b 14. 45.</ns0:note> As thy sword hath made women childless <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Whereby it appears; that he was a cruel Tyrant, and Guilty of many Bloody Actions, and that towards Gods People, though it be not related elsewhere. And this seems to be added for the fuller vindication of Gods justice, and to shew, that although God did at this time remember and revenge a Crime committed by this Mans Ancestors 400 Years ago, yet he did not punish an Innocent Son for his Fa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thers Crimes, but one that allowed and persisted in the same evil courses.</ns0:note>, so shall thy mother be childless among women. And Samuel hewed Agag in pieces <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">This he did by Di<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>ine instinct, and in pur<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />suance of Gods express and particular Command, above, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 3. which being sinfully neglected by <ns0:hi>Saul,</ns0:hi> is now executed by <ns0:hi>Samuel.</ns0:hi> See the like example 1 <ns0:hi>King.</ns0:hi> 18. 40.                   <ns0:p n="34">
